solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Plane just the same going up and down (5)

indicators.text: just the same going up and down
indicators.note: in a down entry, a word that reads identically from the top or from the bottom is a palindrome

blocks.clueFragment: just the same going up and down
blocks.note: describes the letters, not the meaning: a five-letter word whose spelling survives being read upwards

explanation.surface: An aircraft bobbing up and down yet somehow staying put.
explanation.walkthrough: "Plane" looks like an aircraft, and "up and down" plays along with the flight; it is really a flat surface, and the rest describes the letters of a down answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Plane in its geometric, adjectival sense is a plain synonym: a flat, even surface.

clue.text: Staff stood up on excursion at the back (8)

indicators.note: in a down entry, standing a word up makes it read from the bottom, so ROD becomes DOR
in a down clue, the first piece sits on top of the second

blocks.note: a rod is a staff or stick
a sally is an outing or trip

explanation.surface: An employee standing tall at the rear of a coach trip.
explanation.walkthrough: "Staff" suggests employees, but it is a stick. The answer is the adverb from dorsal, as in a fish's dorsal fin.
explanation.definitionFit: Dorsal is the anatomical word for the back, so the adverb means on or at the back.

clue.text: Grey perhaps unlikely to fade? (6)

blocks.note: the surface wants a colour; a grey is also a horse, and 'perhaps' marks it as one example of a kind
not a colour holding fast but a racehorse that does not tire in the closing stages of a long race

explanation.surface: A grey colour that will not wash out.
explanation.walkthrough: "Grey" and "fade" read as dye losing its strength; switch to the racecourse and a horse that won't fade late on is a STAYER.
explanation.definitionFit: Racing jargon: a stayer is a horse with the stamina for long distances, and a grey is one horse by coat colour.

clue.text: Hiccup somewhat nauseating and gassy, first of all (4)

indicators.note: 'first' of 'all' the preceding words: take each word's opening letter

blocks.note: the opening letters of the four words

explanation.surface: Hiccups after a fizzy drink, a little queasy-making.
explanation.walkthrough: "Hiccup" reads as the bodily kind, which suits the gassy surface; here it means a small setback.
explanation.definitionFit: Hiccup in its figurative sense, a small hitch that interrupts progress, is a plain synonym.

clue.text: Six of nine petals in flowering plant (6)

indicators.note: take six consecutive letters from the words that follow
the letters sit inside those words

blocks.note: drop the first two letters of 'nine' and the last two of 'petals'; six remain

explanation.surface: Counting petals on a flower: six of its nine.
explanation.walkthrough: "Six of nine" sounds like arithmetic; it is an instruction to take six letters running through "nine petals". NEPETA is catmint.
explanation.definitionFit: Definition by genus: nepeta is the botanical name for catmint, a flowering herb.

clue.text: Coin drop in fictional game (9)

blocks.note: a quid is a pound coin, British slang
to ditch is to drop or abandon

explanation.surface: Dropping a coin during a game in a novel.
explanation.walkthrough: A quid is British slang for a pound. "In" joins the wordplay to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Definition by example: it is the broomstick sport invented for the Harry Potter books.

clue.text: Gross, as is mutineer? (9)

blocks.note: a mutineer is rising up against authority; the question mark flags the literal reading

explanation.surface: Calling a mutineer disgusting.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags the second sense: a mutineer is literally in revolt.
explanation.definitionFit: Two senses of one word: disgusting, as gross is, and taking part in an uprising, as a mutineer does.

clue.text: Auditor’s one for capital (5)

indicators.note: an auditor is literally a listener, so this is the word as it is heard

blocks.note: a soul is a person, one individual, as in 'not a soul'

explanation.surface: An accountant's single entry for capital.
explanation.walkthrough: "Auditor" and "capital" suggest accounts; an auditor is also a hearer, and capital is a city whose name is said like SOUL.
explanation.definitionFit: Definition by category: the city is the capital of South Korea.

clue.text: Off the rails, like holder of food (6)

blocks.note: as = like, as in 'as a bird'

explanation.surface: A food trolley derailed.
explanation.walkthrough: The comma splits the definition from the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: Idiom: going off the rails is wandering from the proper course, which is going wrong.

clue.text: Lower garment (6)

blocks.note: read as low-er, something that lows: a cow, here one particular breed

explanation.surface: A garment for the lower body.
explanation.walkthrough: "Lower garment" reads as trousers or a skirt, but the answer is worn on top; "Lower" is a cow, the thing that moos.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example for the cow, a Channel Island dairy breed, and a plain synonym for the knitted top.

clue.text: Date with God as yet uncertain! (2,6)

indicators.note: letters that are uncertain are not settled in any fixed order

explanation.surface: Religious doubt about who you are going out with.
explanation.walkthrough: "Date" suggests a day in the calendar; it is a verb, to go out with someone. The irony is that the answer means settled while the indicator says uncertain.
explanation.definitionFit: Idiom: to go steady is to have a regular romantic partner, to date one person.

clue.text: Little bloomer of legend featured in newspaper (6)

indicators.note: a story featured in a paper appears inside it, so LORE goes inside FT

explanation.surface: A newspaper story about a legendary small blunder.
explanation.walkthrough: "Bloomer" suggests a gaffe or old-fashioned underwear; here it is something that blooms.
explanation.definitionFit: A playful sense: a bloomer is anything that blooms, and this is a small flower within a flower head.

clue.text: Sign me up after youngster (5)

indicators.note: in a down entry, a word written upwards reads from the bottom, so ME becomes EM
the reversed word comes after, below, the youngster

blocks.note: a tot is a small child

explanation.surface: Asking to be enrolled after a child has been.
explanation.walkthrough: "Sign me up" reads as enlisting, but "Sign" is the definition and "me up" is ME turned upside down.
explanation.definitionFit: A totem is an emblem that stands for a clan, so a sign in the sense of symbol.

clue.text: Crew member I adore goes abroad (6)

indicators.note: 'abroad' also means astray or scattered widely, so the letters wander out of order

explanation.surface: A sailor I love heading overseas.
explanation.walkthrough: "Crew" suggests a ship, and "goes abroad" keeps up the sailing picture; the crew is a touring band's.
explanation.definitionFit: Definition by example: the crew is a band's road crew, whose members shift the gear on tour.

clue.text: Folly is in a tiny ground (9)

indicators.note: past tense of grind: the letters are ground up and remixed

explanation.surface: A folly, the ornamental building, standing in a small plot of land.
explanation.walkthrough: "Folly" and "ground" suggest a garden folly in its grounds; folly is foolishness, and ground is from grind.
explanation.definitionFit: Plain synonym: being asinine, like an ass, is stupidity, which is folly.

clue.text: Bum say snaffles hot pasty (4)

indicators.note: as an adjective bum means bad or faulty, so the letters of SAY come out wrong
to snaffle is to grab, so the jumbled letters take H inside

blocks.note: H = hot, as on a tap

explanation.surface: A layabout grabbing a hot pastry.
explanation.walkthrough: "Bum" and "pasty" suggest a tramp and a Cornish pie (a pasty is a folded meat pastry); bum is an adjective meaning bad, and pasty is pale-faced.
explanation.definitionFit: Plain synonym: a pasty face is pale, the grey-white colour of ash.

clue.text: Roll barrel slowly at the end (5)

indicators.note: only the end of 'slowly' is used, its final letter

blocks.note: a butt is a large cask

explanation.surface: Rolling a barrel along, slowing down at the finish.
explanation.walkthrough: "Roll" reads as a verb pushing the barrel; it is a bread roll.
explanation.definitionFit: Regional use: in northern England a butty is a sandwich, often in a bread roll, as in chip butty.

clue.text: Arctic element embraced by mammoth (6)

indicators.note: something embraced is held in the arms, so TIN sits inside BIG

explanation.surface: A woolly mammoth frozen in Arctic ice.
explanation.walkthrough: The mammoth and the Arctic make one frozen scene, but "Arctic" is an adjective for bitter cold and "mammoth" just means big.
explanation.definitionFit: Arctic, lower case in sense, describes weather cold enough to sting the skin.

clue.text: Get down – you can get down from one! (4)

definitions.text: you can get down from one!

blocks.clueFragment: you can get down from one!
blocks.note: down here is soft under-feather, and this bird supplies it for eiderdowns

explanation.surface: An order to take cover, plus a note on how to climb down.
explanation.walkthrough: The second "get down" is not a movement at all: down is fine feather.
explanation.definitionFit: Two senses: the verb for dodging low, and a waterbird described by what it yields.

clue.text: Joint vote rubbished within political chamber (8)

indicators.note: to rubbish something is to trash it, so VOTE's letters are scrambled
the scrambled letters go inside DAIL

blocks.note: the Dáil is the lower house of the Irish parliament

explanation.surface: A ballot thrown out in parliament.
explanation.walkthrough: "Joint" in a political surface hints at a joint motion; it is a carpentry joint.
explanation.definitionFit: Definition by example: it is an interlocking woodworking joint shaped like a bird's tail.

clue.text: Piece, obscurity recited? (6)

indicators.note: something recited is spoken, so the answer is how the word sounds

explanation.surface: A poem read out, with an obscure passage.
explanation.walkthrough: "Piece" suggests a recited piece of writing; it is a chess piece.
explanation.definitionFit: Definition by example: one of the chessmen, the one that moves in an L.

clue.text: Maiden route in Irish county (6)

blocks.note: a gal is a girl, a maiden

explanation.surface: A maiden voyage or first road in the west of Ireland.
explanation.walkthrough: "Maiden" reads as first, as in a maiden voyage; here it is a girl. "In" links wordplay to definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Definition by category: a county on Ireland's west coast.

clue.text: Reason this person has to follow cat around (6)

indicators.note: what follows comes after, so I'VE is placed after the cat
turned around to face the other way, so TOM reads MOT

blocks.note: a tom is a male cat
this person = I, the setter; I have = I've

explanation.surface: Someone justifying why they must trail a cat about.
explanation.walkthrough: "This person" is the setter speaking of themself, so I; with "has" it makes I'VE.
explanation.definitionFit: Plain synonym: the reason behind an action, what drives it.

clue.text: Little less than lucid? (6)

blocks.note: a little drunk, so not thinking quite clearly

explanation.surface: Someone who is not quite thinking clearly.
explanation.walkthrough: "Little less than lucid" reads as one phrase, a bit muddled; split it and both halves give one British slang word.
explanation.definitionFit: Two informal British senses: very small, and slightly tipsy.

clue.text: One opens abridged tome and a problem solved! (5)

indicators.note: I splits VOL open by sitting inside it
an abridged text is cut short, so the word for tome is shortened

blocks.note: a tome is a volume, abbreviated to VOL

explanation.surface: Opening a short book and finding the answer to a puzzle.
explanation.walkthrough: VOL is the standard abbreviation of volume. "And" joins wordplay to definition; the answer is French for 'there you are'.
explanation.definitionFit: The French exclamation is used on completing something, like a triumphant 'there!' when a problem is solved.

clue.text: Gag aboard ship binds mouth of engineer (3-5)

indicators.note: to bind is to tie round, so ON LINER wraps around E
the mouth is the opening, so the first letter of engineer

explanation.surface: An engineer bound and gagged on board a ship.
explanation.walkthrough: "Gag" and "binds mouth" paint a hostage; the gag is a joke, and "mouth" is the opening letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Comedy slang: a gag is a joke, and this is a joke delivered in a single line.

clue.text: Cover uncovered evidence (4)

indicators.note: with its cover taken off: in a down entry the top letter is the lid

explanation.surface: Hidden evidence brought to light.
explanation.walkthrough: "Cover uncovered" looks contradictory; the definition is "Cover" and the wordplay is evidence losing its top letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Plain synonym in the sense of shelter: the covering over a building.

clue.text: Too much wine Edward knocked back (2,4)

indicators.note: knocked backwards, so the letters of PORT ED run from the end

explanation.surface: Edward drinking one glass of wine too many.
explanation.walkthrough: "Knocked back" is drinking-talk in the surface; in the wordplay it turns both pieces round together, not each separately.
explanation.definitionFit: A French borrowing meaning superfluous, more than is wanted.

clue.text: Secure components, looking back (5)

indicators.note: looking back runs the eye from the end to the start

explanation.surface: Fastening pieces in place while glancing behind.
explanation.walkthrough: "Secure" is a verb here, to fasten, not the adjective for safe.
explanation.definitionFit: Verb sense: to fasten something down with a band or belt.

clue.text: A cell Fido messed up – the pits there? (9)

indicators.note: made a mess of, so the letters are thrown into disorder

explanation.surface: A dog wrecking its kennel, which is now the pits.
explanation.walkthrough: "The pits" reads as slang for somewhere awful, fitting the wrecked cell; it means coal mines.
explanation.definitionFit: Definition by description: a region where the pits, coal mines, are found; the question mark flags the indirectness.
